evidence.correctness: Re-ran experiments/run.py (101 s): byte-identical to results.txt. Recomputed independently in numpy (scratch ind.py): the full Kronecker second-moment operator over (mode,state) with eigvals instead of the author's power iteration, characteristic-polynomial roots for constant delay, a linear solve for the stationary variance, and a separate vectorised Monte Carlo of the raw recursion and of the Lyapunov exponent. Constant-delay thresholds 2/1/0.618034/0.445042/0.347296 match the closed form; i.i.d. thresholds 1.0000/0.95237/0.66832/0.64207 match; variances 4.017857/4.915201 (k=0.8) and 6.264531/15.152825 (k=0.6, rho=0.9/0.99) match; direct simulation 6.2648 vs 6.2645; kc(kc+1)=1/p holds to 1e-13; a.s. thresholds 1.843 and exponents agree. Only blemish: rho>=0.9 thresholds are 2e-4 to 3e-4 off the exact value in the 4th printed decimal (0.6723 vs 0.67211, 0.6236 vs 0.62337) and d=3,4 numerical column 4e-4 off (disclosed). Numbers are right for the stated model.
evidence.completeness: Claimed: Markov-jump threshold machinery, i.i.d. results, persistence results, variance inflation, the a.s. vs MS contrast, experiments, whitepaper, figure, 8 tests: all present and working. 8 tests pass in 14.2 s (README says about 12 s); run.py takes 101 s (about 90 s). The only figure shows the constant-delay formula check, not the persistence headline. No stubs or TODOs; the whitepaper's next steps are labelled future work. Live page not loaded (no network check).
evidence.verification: `PYTHONPATH=src python3 -m unittest discover -s tests` -> Ran 8 tests OK. Three seeded mutations (reverted, git status clean, files compared with a saved copy): (1) lyapunov ignores persistence, draw(P[mode]) -> draw(probs): all 8 tests pass (not caught); (2) transposed P in _push: pass (not caught; the MS threshold appears spectrum-equivalent so it is partly an equivalent mutant, but stationary_var and non-symmetric cases are unpinned); (3) stationary_var noise weight loses p: caught by the twin-versus-{0,2} variance test. 1 of 3 caught. The tests are good where they use closed forms (constant-delay formula, kc(kc+1)=1/p, twin variance equality, effective_delay inverse) but nothing tests the a.s. simulator under persistence or any non-symmetric marginal with rho>0, and nothing pins results.txt.
evidence.craft: Read src/jitter_twin/model.py (about 170 lines), tests/test_model.py, experiments/run.py and figure.py header. Clean, documented, pure Python with small functions, no dead code, and the monotonicity assumption of the bisection is stated. Defects: pure-Python matrices make run.py 100 s (numpy would be seconds and allow eigvals instead of power iteration); power iteration is fixed at 1500 iterations with no convergence check, biasing thresholds at 2e-4 to 4e-4; no validation of probs or rho; ms_critical_gain returns inf silently if stable at kmax=2.5; the one figure covers section 1 only.
evidence.claims: Every number in the README abstract and whitepaper checked against results.txt: all equal. Limits and 'Stylised' disclaimer present; the empirical status of the kc(kc+1)=1/p fit and of the variance coincidence is stated, as is the one-seed Monte Carlo and the d>=3 4e-4 accuracy. Problems: the whitepaper title 'halves the mean-square gain margin' is not backed (the threshold falls at most 38%, 1.000 to 0.624, floor 0.618); the Builds-on line cites research groups whose papers are not reproduced (disclosed); the closest prior work on Markov-delay jump systems is not cited. The rho-dependent power-iteration bias is undisclosed.
evidence.fitness: A researcher could use the machinery (it is correct and small) and the observation that the delay histogram does not fix mean-square stability, but the contribution is an application of standard MJLS theory to a scalar integrator with an invented delay process, validated against another simulation. Nearest prior work: Nilsson, Bernhardsson & Wittenmark 1998 (Markov and i.i.d. random delay in control loops), Zhang, Branicky & Phillips 2001, Costa-Fragoso-Marques 2005 (second-moment operator is their Theorem), Hespanha et al. 2007 survey. The i.i.d. vs Markov distinction and MS vs a.s. gap are known; what is new is only the sticky-redraw one-parameter sweep and the twin-certification framing. No delay traces, no estimation of rho from data (listed as next step). Not a publishable standalone result at the programme's PhD bar.
evidence.domain: A controls researcher would first ask whether the delay process is realisable (a freshest-sample sensor cannot jump from delay 0 to 2; age grows by one per step), whether a scalar integrator with gain k is representative, and why the sinusoidal-stable-gain bound is the right comparison (it is exact for the stated plant). They would accept the MJLS second-moment method and the MS-versus-a.s. distinction (correct and well explained) and the sticky-redraw construction with exact lag-1 autocorrelation rho. They would want a delay model from queueing or bus data, the distinction between MS and a.s. requirements tied to a real safety criterion, and the Markov-delay literature cited.

defects.what: Tests never exercise lyapunov/as_critical_gain with rho>0, so the a.s. persistence column of results section 3 (and the claim that the a.s. threshold is nearly insensitive to rho) has no test; a seeded mutation that ignores persistence in the simulator passes all 8 tests

Transposing the transition matrix in _push passes every test: persistence tests use the symmetric HALF law, so P equals its transpose (the MS threshold turned out spectrum-equivalent in the cases tried, but stationary_var and non-uniform marginals with rho>0 are unpinned). No test uses a non-uniform marginal with rho>0 or compares to an independent solution

Not new: Markov-jump-linear-system stability of networked control with random and Markov-correlated delay is the subject of Nilsson et al. 1998 and Zhang-Branicky-Phillips 2001 (neither cited); the persistence effect is the known gap between i.i.d. and Markov delay models. The delay is a sticky-redraw chain that can jump 0 to 2 (an older sample than the previous step), the plant is a scalar integrator, and the 'real' system is simulated with no delay trace
Whitepaper title says bursty delay 'halves the mean-square gain margin'; results.txt show a 38% threshold fall at most (1.000 to 0.624), bounded by the constant-delay-2 threshold 0.618

Power iteration under-converges near the threshold: rho=0.9 threshold printed 0.6723 vs exact 0.6721, d=3,4 table 0.444680/0.346901 vs 0.445042/0.347296 (the d>=3 bias is disclosed, the rho bias is not)
Only figure plots the constant-delay formula check, not the persistence result; no test pins results.txt to run.py, no input validation (probs not checked to sum to 1, rho>=1, delays with gaps)
README test and run timings drifted (about 12 s measured 14.2 s, about 90 s measured 101 s)

verdict: The numbers are right: run.py regenerates results.txt byte-identically, and an independent numpy implementation (full Kronecker second-moment operator with eigvals, linear-solve variance, raw-recursion Monte Carlo, independent Lyapunov exponents) reproduces every headline value, the 0.435 crossing and kc(kc+1)=1/p, with only 2e-4 to 4e-4 power-iteration bias in the 4th decimal at high persistence. The README is honest about being stylised. It fails the bar on verification alone: of three seeded mutations the tests missed two, including one that makes the almost-sure simulator ignore delay persistence (the whole a.s.-versus-rho column of result 3 is untested) and one transposing the mode-transition matrix (all persistence tests use a symmetric law). Scores are fitness and domain 2: the result is a standard Markov-jump-system analysis (Nilsson 1998, Zhang-Branicky-Phillips 2001, not cited) on a scalar integrator with a simulated, partly unphysical delay process and no data, and the whitepaper title overstates the effect ('halves' versus at most a 38% fall). Worst defect: the untested persistence path in the a.s. simulator plus the research-design gap of missing prior work and no delay trace. Does not meet the bar (verification 2).
